title: U.S. DOT Refunds — Local summary (not verbatim)
text: A passenger is entitled to a refund of the ticket price when the airline cancels a flight, regardless of the reason, and the passenger chooses not to travel or does not accept travel credits, vouchers, or other compensation offered instead of a refund.

title: U.S. DOT Refunds — Local summary (not verbatim)
section: REFUND AFTER A SIGNIFICANT DELAY OR SCHEDULE CHANGE
text: A passenger is entitled to a refund when an airline significantly delays or significantly changes a flight and the passenger chooses not to travel or does not accept travel credits, vouchers, or other compensation offered instead of a refund.

title: U.S. DOT Refunds — Local summary (not verbatim)
section: WHAT COUNTS AS A SIGNIFICANT DELAY OR CHANGE
text:
For a domestic itinerary, late arrival means the passenger is scheduled to arrive at the destination airport 3 hours or more later than the original scheduled arrival time. For an international itinerary, the threshold is 6 hours or more later than the original scheduled arrival time.

For an early departure, the passenger is scheduled to depart from the origin airport 3 hours or more earlier than the original scheduled departure time for a domestic itinerary, or 6 hours or more earlier for an international itinerary.

Other changes that may qualify include a different origin or destination airport, more connection points than the original itinerary, or an involuntary downgrade. A passenger who continues travel after an involuntary downgrade is generally entitled to the difference between the original fare and the downgraded fare, rather than a refund of the full airfare.

title: U.S. DOT Refunds — Local summary (not verbatim)
section: IMPORTANT: DEPARTURE DELAY IS NOT THE SAME AS LATE ARRIVAL
text: A flight departing 4 hours later than scheduled does not, by itself, establish the DOT late-arrival refund threshold. Compare the originally scheduled arrival time with the newly scheduled arrival time. The domestic late-arrival threshold is based on arriving at least 3 hours later. Do not describe a 3-hour-later departure as the early-departure rule; early departure means leaving earlier than originally scheduled.

title: U.S. DOT Refunds — Local summary (not verbatim)
section: IF THE PASSENGER ACCEPTS OR TAKES ALTERNATIVE TRANSPORTATION
text: A passenger who chooses to take the significantly delayed or changed flight, or an alternative flight offered by the airline, is generally not entitled to a refund of the ticket price under this DOT rule. If a passenger rejects the alternative offer, or does not respond and does not take the alternative transportation, a refund must be issued automatically. Airlines must notify passengers of the right to a refund when offering alternative transportation.

title: U.S. DOT Refunds — Local summary (not verbatim)
text: A required ticket refund is returned to the original form of payment. A voucher, travel credit, or other compensation in place of a refund may be offered, but the passenger must be informed of the refund right and must affirmatively choose to accept the alternative form. The DOT refund page states that credit-card refunds are due within 7 business days, and refunds for other payment methods (such as cash or check) are due within 20 calendar days, subject to the specific event and timing described on the current DOT page. Do not call the 20-day period 20 business days.

title: U.S. DOT Refunds — Local summary (not verbatim)
section: LEGAL REFERENCE — SEE ALSO 14 CFR PART 260
text:
For the regulatory definition of a significantly delayed or changed flight, see 14 CFR §260.2. The definition includes a scheduled late arrival at least 3 hours later for domestic itineraries or at least 6 hours later for international itineraries, and an early departure at least 3 hours earlier for domestic itineraries or 6 hours earlier for international itineraries.

For the carrier's obligation to refund airfare for a cancelled or significantly delayed or changed flight, see 14 CFR §260.6, titled "Refunding fare for flights cancelled or significantly delayed or changed by carriers." The provision addresses a full and prompt refund when a consumer with a nonrefundable ticket chooses not to fly on the significantly delayed or changed flight, accept an alternative flight, or accept a voucher, credit, or other compensation offered in place of the refund.

title: U.S. DOT Refunds — Local summary (not verbatim)
section: LEGAL REFERENCE — SEE ALSO 14 CFR PART 260
text: The current eCFR links are https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-14/chapter-II/subchapter-A/part-260/section-260.2 and https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-14/chapter-II/subchapter-A/part-260/section-260.6. The eCFR page displayed the current Title 14 content as of October 29, 2026. Do not cite 14 CFR §250.13 as the refund rule; the refund provisions described here are in Part 260.

title: U.S. DOT Refunds — Local summary (not verbatim)
text: This is an educational local summary, not legal advice. Do not infer refund eligibility from a departure delay alone. Establish the itinerary type, original and revised scheduled arrival times, whether the passenger accepts or uses alternative transportation, and whether the passenger chooses not to travel. Refer to the linked official DOT and eCFR pages for all details and exceptions.

title: U.S. DOT Tarmac Delays — Local summary (not verbatim)
text: A tarmac delay occurs when an aircraft is on the ground, either waiting to take off or after landing, and passengers do not have an opportunity to get off the plane. The DOT tarmac-delay rule applies to covered carriers at U.S. airports. Waiting in the terminal or at a gate is not, by itself, a tarmac delay.

title: U.S. DOT Tarmac Delays — Local summary (not verbatim)
text:
For flights departing from a U.S. airport, airlines must begin moving the aircraft to a place where passengers can safely get off before 3 hours for domestic flights and before 4 hours for international flights. For arriving flights landing at U.S. airports, passengers must be given an opportunity to safely get off before 3 hours for domestic flights and before 4 hours for international flights.

Exceptions to the time limits are allowed for safety, security, or air-traffic-control reasons. Passengers should not leave the aircraft unless the airline tells them it is safe. The airline is not required to let a passenger back on the aircraft after the passenger chooses to get off during a tarmac delay.

title: U.S. DOT Tarmac Delays — Local summary (not verbatim)
text: During a covered tarmac delay, airlines must provide a snack and drinking water no later than 2 hours after the start of the tarmac delay. The rule does not require a full meal during a tarmac delay. Food and water may be withheld only when the pilot determines service cannot be provided for safety or security reasons.

title: U.S. DOT Tarmac Delays — Local summary (not verbatim)
text: During a tarmac delay, airlines must provide working toilets, comfortable cabin temperatures, and adequate medical attention when needed. Airlines must notify passengers about the status of the delay when the tarmac delay exceeds 30 minutes. If passengers can safely leave, the airline must timely notify them of the opportunity.

title: U.S. DOT Tarmac Delays — Local summary (not verbatim)
text: The 3-hour domestic and 4-hour international limits concern the opportunity to leave an aircraft during a covered tarmac delay. They do not mean that every 3- or 4-hour delay while waiting in an airport terminal automatically creates a federal right to a hotel or meal under the tarmac-delay rule. For terminal delays, check the airline's customer-service commitments and the separate DOT refund rules.

title: U.S. DOT Airline Customer Service Dashboard — American Airlines local summary (not verbatim)
text: The U.S. DOT dashboard describes services airlines commit to provide when a delay or cancellation is caused by circumstances within the airline's control. Examples given by DOT include maintenance or crew problems, cabin cleaning, baggage loading, and fueling. These commitments should not be described as automatic benefits for every delay, including delays caused by weather or other circumstances outside airline control.

title: U.S. DOT Airline Customer Service Dashboard — American Airlines local summary (not verbatim)
text:
The dashboard marks American Airlines as committed to rebook passengers on the same airline at no additional cost for significant controllable delays.

The dashboard marks American Airlines as committed to rebook passengers on a partner airline, or another airline with which it has an agreement, at no additional cost for significant controllable delays.

The dashboard marks American Airlines as committed to provide a meal or meal cash/voucher when a flight delay results in a passenger waiting 3 hours or more. This is a waiting-time condition for meal assistance. It is not the federal refund threshold and must not be confused with the late-arrival test used by the DOT refund rule.

The dashboard marks American Airlines as committed to complimentary hotel accommodations and ground transportation to and from the hotel for passengers affected by an overnight controllable delay.

title: U.S. DOT Airline Customer Service Dashboard — American Airlines local summary (not verbatim)
text: The dashboard does not mark American Airlines as committed to cash compensation, a credit or travel voucher, or frequent-flyer miles when a controllable delay results in a passenger waiting 3 hours or more from the scheduled departure time. Do not convert this absence of a dashboard commitment into a claim that a passenger can never receive a discretionary offer or other remedy under a different rule or policy.

title: U.S. DOT Airline Customer Service Dashboard — American Airlines local summary (not verbatim)
section: IMPORTANT DISTINCTION — REFUND VS. SERVICE COMMITMENT
text: A federal DOT refund right is separate from an airline's service commitments. For a domestic itinerary, the refund significant-delay test is based on scheduled arrival at least 3 hours later than the original scheduled arrival time, and the passenger must choose not to travel or accept the alternative offered. The AA meal commitment instead uses a wait of 3 hours or more. A 4-hour arrival delay does not by itself prove that the passenger waited 3 hours at the airport; assess the actual waiting condition separately.

title: U.S. DOT Airline Customer Service Dashboard — American Airlines local summary (not verbatim)
section: SIGNIFICANT DELAY IS NOT A UNIVERSAL 3-HOUR RULE
text: The dashboard describes no-cost rebooking for "significant delays" but does not set a universal numeric 3-hour definition for every significant controllable delay. Do not infer such a definition from the separate 3-hour meal-wait commitment or from the federal refund threshold.

title: U.S. DOT Airline Customer Service Dashboard — American Airlines local summary (not verbatim)
text: The U.S. DOT dashboard states that airlines are required to adhere to the promises in their customer service plans and that DOT will hold airlines accountable if they fail to fulfill a commitment. DOT advises passengers to contact the airline first; if dissatisfied with the airline's response or conduct, the passenger may file a complaint with DOT. Do not claim that enforcement is exclusively internal or that DOT has no role in accountability.

title: U.S. DOT Airline Customer Service Dashboard — American Airlines local summary (not verbatim)
text: This is an educational local summary, not legal advice. The dashboard is a summary of airline commitments, not a statement that every delay qualifies. Check the live DOT dashboard and American Airlines customer service plan for any later changes before presenting this summary as current policy.

title: eCFR — 14 CFR §260.2 Significant Delay Definition (local summary)
text: 14 CFR §260.2 defines a "significantly delayed or changed flight" for purposes of the refund rules in Part 260. Relevant triggers include a scheduled arrival at least 3 hours after the original scheduled arrival for a domestic itinerary, or at least 6 hours after the original scheduled arrival for an international itinerary.

title: eCFR — 14 CFR §260.2 Significant Delay Definition (local summary)
text: The same definition includes a flight scheduled to depart at least 3 hours earlier than its original scheduled departure for a domestic itinerary, or at least 6 hours earlier for an international itinerary. An early departure is different from a departure that is merely late.

title: eCFR — 14 CFR §260.2 Significant Delay Definition (local summary)
text: The definition also includes specified changes such as a different origin or destination airport, more connection points, or an involuntary downgrade, subject to the detailed rule text and applicable conditions.

title: eCFR — 14 CFR §260.2 Significant Delay Definition (local summary)
text: For the definition of a significantly delayed or changed flight, cite 14 CFR §260.2. For the carrier's refund obligation after cancellation or significant delay/change, see the separate 14 CFR §260.6 source. Do not cite 14 CFR §250.13 as the refund authority.

title: eCFR — 14 CFR §260.6 Refund Obligation (local summary)
text: 14 CFR §260.6 addresses a covered carrier's obligation to provide a full and prompt refund of airfare, including taxes and ancillary fees, for a cancelled or significantly delayed or changed flight when the consumer chooses not to fly on the affected flight or accept rebooking on an alternative flight, and does not accept a voucher, credit, or other compensation offered in place of the refund.

title: eCFR — 14 CFR §260.6 Refund Obligation (local summary)
text: Section 260.6(a)(2) describes situations in which the refund is due automatically, including when a consumer rejects the significantly delayed or changed flight, an alternative flight, or an offer of voucher, credit, or other compensation. It also covers specified cases where the consumer does not respond to an offer and does not use the offered transportation.

title: eCFR — 14 CFR §260.6 Refund Obligation (local summary)
text: Section 260.6(c) allows a covered carrier to offer a voucher, credit, or other compensation as an explicit alternative to a required refund only with clear and conspicuous notice of the consumer's right to a full refund and other stated conditions. Do not say a passenger automatically loses a refund simply because the airline mentions a voucher; the consumer must affirmatively accept the alternative compensation under the applicable rules.

title: eCFR — 14 CFR §260.6 Refund Obligation (local summary)
text: The definition of a "significantly delayed or changed flight," including the 3-hour domestic and 6-hour international late-arrival thresholds, is in 14 CFR §260.2. See https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-14/chapter-II/subchapter-A/part-260/section-260.2.

title: eCFR — 14 CFR §260.6 Refund Obligation (local summary)
text: For the carrier's refund obligation, cite 14 CFR §260.6. For the definition of a significantly delayed or changed flight, cite 14 CFR §260.2. Do not cite 14 CFR §250.13 as the refund authority. The linked U.S. DOT Refunds page provides public-facing guidance about these rules.
